results.content: The proposed one-pot COVID-19 detection method consisted of three distinct reactions: (1) reverse transcription of the SARS-CoV-2 RNA to generate complementary DNA, (2) amplification of the resulting DNA using a recombinase polymerase amplification, and (3) perform collateral activity on a reporter probe using CRISPR/Cas12 in the presence of the target DNA fragment; these reactions are summarized in Figure2. ### The First Round of Definitive Screening Design (DSD) for RT-RPA-CRISPR The proposed one-pot detection method, involving three separate reactions, has many factors with the potential to influence performance as shown in Figure2. In a standard reverse transcription protocol, the use of an RNase inhibitor and dithiothreitol (DTT) was recommended by the manufacturers.35,38 The RNase inhibitor is used to block any RNase activity resulting from contamination in the reaction mix,39 and DTT is a reducing agent for disulfide bonds used to stabilize enzymatic activity and indirectly preserve the RNA template.40 However, the use of RNase inhibitor and/or RT buffer containing DTT and other compounds for a suitable reaction condition is generally omitted in one-pot RT-RPA-based detection reactions.16,17,41 Therefore, RNase inhibitor and RT buffer were included as factors in the screening design to investigate whether their addition could have a positive effect on the response (relative fluorescence unit, RFU). For RT-RPA-CRISPR, the following parameters were used: * 10 U/μL reverse transcriptase, M-MuLV * 0.5× reverse transcription buffer * 0.8 U/μL RNase inhibitor * 1000 nm Cas12a/gRNA complex * 8 μM reporter DNA (ssDNA F-Q reporter) Although the second DSD revealed that increasing the reverse transcriptase concentration and reaction volume were favorable for high fluorescence yields, the values of these factors were not further increased. To determine the lowest detectable copy number of the DNA template, the following parameters suggested by the models were used in the RPA-CRISPR method: * 1000 nm Cas12a/gRNA complex * 10 μM reporter DNA (ssDNA F-Q reporter) As the RPA-CRISPR method targeting a DNA template has a less crowded environment compared to RT-RPA-CRISPR, higher sensitivity was obtained with 0.5 copy/μL (_p_< 0.05) in 40 min for all replicates using a plate reader (Figure9B).

Title: Rational Design of CRISPR/Cas12a-RPA Based One-Pot COVID-19 Detection with Design of Experiments | ACS Synthetic Biology
Here, statistical design of experiments (DoE) was employed to accelerate the development and optimization of a CRISPR/Cas12a-RPA-based one-pot detection method for the first time. The proposed one-pot COVID-19 detection method consisted of three distinct reactions: (1) reverse transcription of the SARS-CoV-2 RNA to generate complementary DNA, (2) amplification of the resulting DNA using a recombinase polymerase amplification, and (3) perform collateral activity on a reporter probe using CRISPR/Cas12 in the presence of the target DNA fragment; these reactions are summarized in Figure 2. In this study, the design of experiments guided reaction optimization improved assay sensitivity, facilitating the detection of just two copies of the COVID-19 RNA genome and 0.5 copies of the COVID-19 DNA fragment per μL. Fluorescence emissions from the tubes containing cDNA products from different copy numbers of SARS-CoV-2 genome after reverse transcription reaction followed by CRISPR/Cas12a assay. As outlined in more detail in the introduction, the one-pot COVID-19 detection method used in this study involved three sequential reactions: reverse transcription (RT), recombinase polymerase amplification (RPA), and CRISPR/Cas12 assay. | condition | dNTP mix (mM) | RNase inhibitor (U/μL) | RT buffer (X) | Cas12a/gRNA (nM) | reporter DNA (μM) | reaction volume (μL) | incubation time | temperature (°C) | relative fluorescence unit (RFU) |. This study aimed to determine differences in the optimal conditions for the one-pot RT-RPA-CRISPR and RPA-CRISPR methods and to expand the optimization of this CRISPR-based one-pot detection method for DNA virus applications. As the RPA-CRISPR method targeting a DNA template has a less crowded environment compared to RT-RPA-CRISPR, higher sensitivity was obtained with 0.5 copy/μL (*p* < 0.05) in 40 min for all replicates using a plate reader (Figure 9B). Most tests for early detection of SARS-CoV-2 RNA rely on the reverse transcription-polymerase chain reaction, but isothermal nucleic acid amplification assays, including transcription-mediated amplification and CRISPR-based methodologies, are promising alternatives. We tried to develop a one-tube detection platform based on RT-RPA (Reverse Transcription and Recombinase Polymerase Isothermal Amplification) and DNA Endonuclease-Targeted CRISPR Trans Reporter (DETECTR) technol., termed OR-DETECTR, to detect SARS-CoV-2. results.title: Current Challenges and Limitations of CRISPR-Target Technology
results.content: Published Time: 2025-05-26T01:28:42+00:00 Current Challenges and Limitations of CRISPR-Target Technology - GenRna Vision Current Challenges and Limitations of CRISPR-Target Technology **Current Challenges and Limitations of CRISPR-Target Technology (2025 Update)** CRISPR-Target technology demonstrates exceptional sensitivity, specificity, and programmability in food safety applications. Off-Target Effects and False Positives** * Trans-cleavage activity of CRISPR-Cas systems (e.g., Cas12, Cas13) may inadvertently degrade non-target nucleic acids or non-nucleic molecules, particularly in complex food matrices. * Low-concentration targets require pre-amplification (e.g., LAMP, RPA), which risks cross-contamination and complicates temperature compatibility with Cas proteins. * Non-nucleic acid targets (e.g., heavy metals, small-molecule toxins) rely on aptamer/DNAzyme signal conversion, but food matrix interference reduces sensitivity by orders of magnitude. * Most CRISPR systems are restricted to single-target detection. * Few countries have established certification protocols for CRISPR-based antibiotic resistance gene screening (e.g.,_blaCTX-M_). * Consumer distrust of CRISPR-edited foods (e.g., hypoallergenic wheat, disease-resistant crops) persists, with demands for mandatory labeling lacking global consensus. Sample Handling and Matrix Interference** * Highly processed foods (e.g., UHT-treated dairy) suffer from DNA degradation, increasing false negatives. * High-fat/protein foods (e.g., meat) inhibit CRISPR reactions, necessitating nanoparticle or magnetic bead enrichment. * CRISPR biosensors exhibit signal drift (e.g., 15% instability) in dynamic environments like cold-chain logistics. ### **Future Directions** * Develop PAM-free Cas variants (e.g., Cas14a) and AI-optimized gRNA design for single-step, amplification-free detection. * Establish universal CRISPR reference materials and mutual recognition of the EU’s _Gene-Edited Food Testing Standards_. * WHO’s _CRISPR Food Safety Guidelines_ advocate open-source technology sharing and public education to boost acceptance. results.title: Designing Guide RNA for CRISPR Genome Editing
results.content: # Designing Guide RNA for CRISPR Genome Editing. At the core of this innovation is guide RNA (gRNA), a molecule that directs the CRISPR system to its exact genomic target. In this article, we explore the essential principles and strategies for designing guide RNA in CRISPR. * Guide RNA (gRNA) directs CRISPR enzymes to specific DNA targets, enabling precise editing. * Effective gRNA design balances target specificity and efficiency, considering factors like GC content, PAM sequence, chromatin accessibility, and seed sequence. Guide RNA (gRNA) is a short RNA molecule that acts as a guide to direct CRISPR enzymes to specific spots in the genome. * **crRNA (CRISPR RNA)**: Contains a spacer sequence (17-21 nucleotides) that targets DNA. ### **Role of Guide RNA in CRISPR Genome Editing**. The guide RNA’s spacer region pairs with the target DNA sequence, locating the correct site for editing. Once the target DNA is found, Cas9 creates a single-strand break in the DNA, aided by the guide RNA. Understanding the fundamental role of guide RNA in directing CRISPR enzymes sets the foundation for exploring how to design these molecular guides effectively for your specific genome editing goals. ## **Design Principles for Guide RNA in CRISPR**. The first step in designing guide RNA (gRNA) is selecting a unique target sequence in the genome. * **Benchling CRISPR Guide RNA Design Tool**: Visualizes, optimizes, and annotates hundreds of gRNAs at once. Once you’ve identified the optimal gRNA sequence using these sophisticated design platforms, the next critical decision involves choosing the most appropriate method to synthesize and deliver your guide RNA. These unwanted edits happen when the gRNA binds to similar but non-target DNA sequences. Designing effective guide RNAs involves many factors, including target specificity, delivery methods, and off-target detection. Our comprehensive transcriptome analysis helps you validate guide RNA designs, assess editing efficiency, and understand the broader impact of your genome modifications with ease. Designing guide RNA is key to successful CRISPR editing, requiring careful attention to target specificity, PAM sequences, delivery methods, and off-target effects. A gRNA sequence can target a conserved region, but its efficiency varies by cell type due to differences in chromatin accessibility, DNA repair, and metabolism.
